messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The storm had come without warning on a late August afternoon, a sudden, violent wall of wind and water that had torn through the trailer park where Marcus lived with his mother. He was seventeen then, two years ago, and he remembered the sound most of all—a deep, grinding roar that seemed to come from everywhere at once, followed by the terrible, wet splintering of wood. He had been in his room, and in the seconds before the wall gave way, he had smelled the strange, metallic tang of rain mixed with overturned earth and something else, something chemical and sharp, from the storage shed that had been ripped apart. The images came back to him now not as a story he could tell, but as a series of still photographs that slammed into his mind without warning: the ceiling bowing inward, his mother’s face in the hallway, the overturned refrigerator blocking the door. When he thought about that afternoon, he could feel the same terror in his chest, the same cold paralysis that had frozen him in place as the water rose around his ankles.

Now, at nineteen, Marcus worked the fry station at a burger chain on the edge of town. The job was supposed to be simple, predictable, but the environment had become a minefield. The moment a customer’s voice raised in impatience, or a manager snapped an order, his heart would hammer and his palms would go slick. He had come to believe that any stressful situation could unravel him completely, and so he had learned to avoid them with a careful, almost ritualistic precision. Before every shift, he would stand in the walk-in cooler and rehearse exactly what he would say to his coworkers, running through possible questions and his responses until the words felt automatic. He had stopped talking to the customers altogether, and when the drive-thru got busy, he would ask to be moved to the back, claiming a headache. His coworkers had stopped inviting him to hang out after work, and he had stopped caring.

What frightened Marcus most was not the memory itself, but the person he had become since it. He used to be the one who made his mother laugh, who cracked jokes at the dinner table, who looked forward to weekends. Now he felt like a stranger in his own body. He had come to believe that the storm had changed something fundamental inside him, something that could not be fixed. The person he was now—quiet, watchful, always bracing for the next bad thing—felt unrecognisable. He was certain that the damage was permanent, that the happy, easygoing version of himself had been washed away along with the trailer. He tried not to think about the storm at all, pushing the images down as soon as they surfaced, but the effort left him exhausted and hollow. When he came home from work, he would sit in the dark of his new apartment, a small studio his mother had helped him afford, and he would feel nothing but a dull, grinding misery. He had stopped answering her calls.

What finally brought Marcus to the clinic was a small, practical failure. He had been scheduled to cover a Saturday shift, and the thought of the weekend crowd, of the noise and the heat and the unpredictable demands, had sent him into a spiral of dread so intense that he had called in sick for three days straight. His manager had left a voicemail saying that if he missed another shift, he would be let go. Marcus had sat on his couch, staring at the phone, and he had realised that he could not keep living this way—not because he wanted to get better, but because he could not afford to lose the job. He was terrified of what therapy might mean, of having to talk about the storm and the smell and the pictures in his head, but he was more afraid of what would happen if he kept going as he was. He wanted, more than anything, to feel like himself again, though he was not sure that version of himself still existed.
